title: Welcome to Blogkit: What You Get Out of the Box
text:
Quarto already makes a good blog: write Markdown, get a listing page, RSS and search. Blogkit adds the parts that usually need a CMS, without a server or a database. This sample site is built with it, so everything below is something you can click on.

What Is Included

Dark and light theme with a toggle in the navbar. Dark is the default and the choice is remembered.
Archive and tag cloud in the sidebar of every post and on the homepage.
Tags page (tags.html#tag=quarto) listing the posts for a tag, with pagination.
Related posts under each post, picked from shared tags and categories.
Author pages and cards: bios and photos kept in one authors.yml.
Hint and reveal buttons for exercise posts (see Exercises with Hints).
A publish script that renders, commits and pushes in one command.



How It Works in One Paragraph
Before every render, a small Python script reads the front matter of all your posts and writes one data file. A browser script loads that file on each page and builds the archive, tag cloud, related posts and author pages. Because the data is rebuilt on any render, adding a post means rendering only that post: older pages pick up the change the next time they are opened.


Your First Post
Create posts/my-first-post.qmd:
---
title: "My First Post"
description: "One sentence for the card and search results."
date: "2026-10-05"
categories: [Notes]
tags: [hello, quarto]
author: "Avery Kestrel"
---

Hello! This post shows up in the archive, under the tags "hello" and "quarto",
and in the author page for Avery Kestrel.
Render it with quarto render posts/my-first-post.qmd, or publish with ./publish.sh posts/my-first-post.qmd. The next posts explain tags and related posts, authors, publishing and theming.






Tip



Every page of this sample site works offline too: open docs/index.html straight from disk and the widgets still load.

title: Exercise Posts: Hint and Reveal Buttons for Code
text:
When a post teaches by exercise, showing the solution straight away spoils it. Blogkit hides the code by default and adds two buttons above it: See hint and Reveal code. Readers can try first, peek at the steps, then compare.

The Markup
Wrap the hint and the code in a reveal-code div:
::: {.reveal-code}
::: {.hint}
- Start `i` at 2.
- Repeat while `i <= 10`.
- Print `i`, then add 2.
:::

```python
i = 2
while i <= 10:
    print(i, end=" ")
    i += 2
```
:::


Live Example
Exercise: print the even numbers from 2 to 10 with a while loop.
Expected output:
2 4 6 8 10



Start a counter i at 2.
Repeat while i <= 10.
Print i, then add 2 to move to the next even number.


i = 2
while i <= 10:
    print(i, end=" ")
    i += 2
print()



Good Habits for Exercise Posts

Show the expected output in the open, so readers know what they are aiming for.
Write hints as short steps, not as the answer in disguise.
Add a “Try next” line with a harder variation.
Run the solution yourself and paste the real output.

Without JavaScript the hint and the code simply stay visible, so nothing is lost for readers who block scripts. Styling for the buttons lives in the extension stylesheet; see Customising the Theme to change it.

title: Authors and Profiles: One YAML File for Bios and Photos
text:
A multi-author blog needs more than a name in the byline. Blogkit keeps profiles in one file and builds everything else from it.

The Profile File
jordan-alder:                       # the slug: authors/jordan-alder.html
  name: Jordan Alder
  aliases: []                       # other spellings used in posts
  image: img/jordan-alder.svg       # square-ish photo, shown as a circle
  tagline: Teaches with code, themes and exercises
  bio: >-
    Jordan builds learning material: exercises with hints, readable themes
    and small examples that run.
  links:
    - {text: Website, href: "https://example.org/jordan"}
Posts keep a plain author: "Jordan Alder" in their front matter. A post belongs to the profile whose name or aliases match, so you can add profiles later without touching old posts.


What You Get

An author page (authors/jordan-alder.html) with the photo, bio, links and all of the author’s posts.
Clickable bylines on post pages and on the homepage cards.
An author card at the end of every post with a link to “All N posts by …”.
Filters and pagination on the author page: pick a category or a tag to narrow the list, then page through ten posts at a time. The state is kept in the address (#cat=Blogkit&page=2), so a filtered view can be shared.



Adding an Author

Add an entry to authors.yml and put the photo in img/.
Run quarto render. Blogkit writes authors/<slug>.qmd for you (never edit that file by hand) and the page is built.
Use the exact name in the posts’ author: field.

An author who is not in authors.yml simply has no link, so guest posts still work.
This sample site has two authors, so you can see both pages and the filters in action. For how the data file reaches the browser, read Welcome to Blogkit.

title: Customising the Theme: CSS Variables and the Dark/Light Toggle
text:
Blogkit ships a dark, high-contrast look with a light alternative. Quarto adds the toggle to the navbar and remembers the reader’s choice; the extension supplies the styles.

How Quarto Switches Themes
The extension sets two themes:
theme:
  dark: [cosmo, theme-dark.scss]
  light: cosmo
Two details are easy to miss. First, the first one listed is the default, so dark loads first. Second, Quarto decides whether a scheme is dark from its background colour, not its name. The tiny theme-dark.scss only sets a near-black $body-bg, which is what makes Quarto treat it as dark. If both entries were plain cosmo, both would count as light and the toggle would appear to do nothing.


The Colour Variables
Almost every colour in the stylesheet comes from a few variables at the top of styles.css:
:root{
  --bk-bg:     #05070d;   /* page background */
  --bk-bg2:    #0a0f1e;   /* panels and cards */
  --bk-cyan:   #00e5ff;   /* main accent */
  --bk-purple: #a855f7;
  --bk-pink:   #ff2fb4;
  --bk-text:   #e8ecf7;
  --bk-muted:  #9aa4c2;
}
In light mode the same names get lighter values (under :root:has(body.quarto-light)), so one variable name works in both schemes. To retheme, change the accent colours in both places.


Replace the Sample Logo
The navbar shows a sample logo, img/logo.svg. Replace it with your own by overwriting that file, or point the logo: setting in _quarto.yml at another image:
website:
  navbar:
    logo: img/logo.svg


Add Your Own Styles
Put extra CSS in your project (for example custom.css) and list it after the format:
format:
  blogkit-html:
    css: custom.css
Use the variables instead of fixed colours:
.my-banner{
  background: var(--bk-bg2);
  border: 1px solid var(--bk-line);
  color: var(--bk-text);
}
A component written this way looks right in dark and light with no extra rules. When you do need a light-only tweak, scope it with body.quarto-light .my-banner { ... }.


Dark Bands on a Light Page
In light mode the navbar and the post title banner stay dark, which gives the page a strong frame. They do this by re-declaring the dark palette on those elements, a trick you can reuse for any section you want to keep dark.


Language and Labels
Interface text (“Archive”, “Tags”, “Related posts”) can be translated or reworded in _quarto.yml:
blogkit:
  labels:
    archive: Archiv
    tags: Schlagworte
    related: Weitere Beiträge
After a theme change, run ./publish.sh --all once so every page gets the new stylesheet; see Publishing with One Command.

title: Publishing with One Command: render, commit, push
text:
Publishing by hand means the same four steps every time: render, check, commit, push. publish.sh does them in one line.

Daily Use
./publish.sh posts/my-new-post.qmd                  # one post
./publish.sh posts/a.qmd posts/b.qmd                # several posts
./publish.sh --all                                  # whole site
./publish.sh -m "Add the tags post" posts/tags.qmd  # custom commit message
./publish.sh --no-push posts/draft.qmd              # render and commit, look first
With no arguments it skips rendering and just refreshes the data file, then commits and pushes whatever is pending.


What the Script Does

Finds the Quarto project (the folder with _quarto.yml).
Renders each file you name. quarto render takes one file per call, so the script loops.
Stages the project folder only, so unrelated changes elsewhere in the repository are left alone.
Stops if a render fails, and skips the commit when nothing changed.
Runs git pull --rebase --autostash and then git push.



Why One Post Is Enough
Blogkit rebuilds its data file on every render, even of a single post. The archive, tags and related posts on all other pages read from that file in the browser, so you never have to re-render the whole site after adding one post. A full --all render is only needed after you change the theme, the stylesheet’s structure or _quarto.yml.


Setting Up GitHub Pages
The sample project builds into docs/. In your repository go to Settings, Pages, choose the main branch and the /docs folder. Because the built HTML is committed, GitHub needs no build step and Quarto does not have to be installed there.


Preview Before You Push
cd docs
python3 -m http.server 8000     # then open http://localhost:8000
Use a hard refresh so the browser does not show stale files. If you like changing things first and publishing later, see Customising the Theme.

title: Writing Posts with Tags, Categories and Related Posts
text:
Everything Blogkit shows comes from the front matter at the top of each post. Four fields matter most.
---
title: "Required"
date: "2026-10-02"                # required, YYYY-MM-DD
categories: [Blogkit, Writing]    # broad: shown on cards, used for filtering
tags: [front-matter, tags]        # specific: drives the tag cloud and related posts
author: "Avery Kestrel"           # matches a name in authors.yml
---
A post without title or date is skipped (a warning is printed while rendering), and draft: true keeps a post out of the archive and tags.

Categories Versus Tags









Categories
Tags




Scope
Broad: language, subject, type
Specific: the concept in this post


Example
Tutorial, R
front-matter, pagination


Where you see them
Cards and the homepage category cloud
Sidebar tag cloud, tags page, post footer


How many
1 to 3
3 to 6



Keep tags lowercase and hyphenated (related-posts, not Related Posts). Blogkit lowercases them anyway, but consistent names mean one tag instead of three near-duplicates.


How Related Posts Are Chosen
Under every post you see up to five related ones. Blogkit scores each other post by the tags and categories it shares with the current one. A shared feature counts for more when few posts have it, so a rare tag such as related-posts says more than a common one such as quarto. Categories count half as much as tags. Posts with no overlap are never shown, so a post with unusual tags may have fewer than five.
In practice: reuse a tag when two posts really are about the same thing, and add one specific tag to every post. Related posts improve as your tagging does.


Where Tags Appear

The sidebar tag cloud, sized by how many posts use each tag.
The tags page: click a tag to see its posts, ten per page by default (per-page: in _quarto.yml).
A Tags row under each post body.
